question: In its reply to my written question E-001503/20261, the Commission stated that safeguard measures on four alloying elements, not including silicon, were imposed on 18 November 2025.

It did, however, admit that ‘the situation has become very difficult in the meantime’, further stating, therefore, that the Commission services remained available ‘to explore together with the industry, the availability of any possible options under the trade defence instruments.

’ The fact is that no measures have been taken; workers at Spain’s only silicon metal production plant are still on a temporary lay-off scheme, and Europe risks losing this key industry in the wake of the flood of imports from China and African countries such as Angola sold on the European market at knock-down prices. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What it has done since then, and when does it intend to adopt safeguard measures to protect production of silicon metal?

Will the Commission continue to allow the production of a critical and strategic material, as set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/125, such as silicon metal, to collapse within the Union, thereby increasing our external dependence?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.11.2026) On 1 September 2026, the Commission initiated a review of the anti-dumping measures currently in force against imports of silicon metal imports from China, in order to assess under Article 11(3) of the basic Anti-dumping Regulation1 if the current measures are still sufficient to counteract the injurious dumping.

If the Commission assesses that the level of the current measures is not sufficient to address the damage caused by unfairly low-priced imports, it will increase such level to provide additional protection to the EU producers of silicon metal, if the relevant conditions are met.

Moreover, the Commission remains available to analyse any additional data and evidence relating to the production of silicon metal in the EU in order to explore, together with the industry, what other possibilities are available in the field of trade defence, including possible safeguard measures.

In order to initiate a trade defence investigation, the Commission needs the cooperation from the industry which is required to provide in particular data regarding its economic situation. When, subsequently, it comes to the imposition of safeguard measures, Member States need to vote by qualified majority.
